list.listitem: Yearly influenza vaccination is recommended by ACIP (US) for persons over the age of 6 months. A

Patients classically present with rapid onset of fever, cough, chills or rigors, sore throat, and myalgias. A clinical decision rule can be used to identify patients at low, moderate or high risk of influenza. B
Rapid antigen tests are most useful during the beginning and end of the flu season. C

Treatment is largely supportive; antiviral medications are recommended only if the likelihood of influenza is high and the patient presents within 24 hours of symptom onset. There is no evidence that they reduce serious complications or hospitalization. A
Predictors of adverse outcome in the elderly include increased age, previous hospitalization, comorbidities, gender, and number of outpatient visits in the previous year (). A

background.definition: Influenza is an acute lower respiratory tract infection with systemic manifestations caused by influenza virus and occurring most frequently in epidemics during the winter months.

list.listitem: Onset of the flu season varies but typically begins at about week 40 of the year in the northern hemisphere (early October) and peaks in January.
Pneumonia and influenza typically cause between 6% and 8% of deaths in the United States but may exceed that during epidemic conditions.
Influenza A (typically 70%-98%).
Influenza B (typically 2%-30%).
Balance between influenza A and B varies from year to year. During 2006/2007 season, 79% were influenza A and 21% were influenza B.
Influenza is caused by single-stranded RNA viruses of the family Orthomyxoviridae.

Hemagglutinin and neuraminidase are surface proteins important in diagnosis and treatment. The subtype is used to describe the virus, that is, H5N1 (avian flu) is hemagglutinin 5 and neuraminidase 1. The so-called "swine flu" is H1N1. Avian flu is discussed in more detail in a separate chapter.
Influenza A typically causes a more severe clinical illness than influenza B.
Persons are infectious from just before the onset of symptoms until 5 to 10 days after the onset of symptoms. Shedding is prolonged in children.
ACIP (United States) recommends influenza vaccination for all persons over the age of 6 months. A

While zanamivir and oseltamivir prevent flu in close contacts and family members (NNT = 25-36), the cost and concerns about developing resistance argue against routine or widespread use for this indication, particularly in vaccinated individuals. A

Influenza vaccination is recommended by ACIP (US) for all persons over the age of 6 months. A Cochrane review found a 3% absolute risk reduction in the likelihood of influenza symptoms (1% vs. 4%) when there was a good match to the circulating virus, but only a 1% reduction when the match was poor.
Vaccination reduced time off work but there is no evidence of an impact on hospitalization or complications. Overall, there is good evidence that immunization is cost-effective.

Vaccination is usually recommended for anyone living in a nursing home or chronic care facility and anyone who lives with or cares for patients at high risk of complications. However, it is unclear if offering vaccination to health care workers in long-term care facilities improves outcomes for residents.
Vaccination is recommended by the CDC and ACIP for pregnant women, and is not associated with any subsequent illness in offspring based on a Canadian registry study.
Live and inactivated vaccines appear effective in healthy children 3 to 16 years of age in preventing influenza and influenza-like illness.

A large observational study found that same-day administration of the COVID-19 vaccine (BNT162b2-biv [Pfizer BioNTech]) and the SIV in the community setting during the 2022–2023 fall and winter seasons in the United States showed similar effectiveness against adverse health outcomes compared with giving each vaccine separately.

Similarly, vaccination appears effective in patients 65 years and older in preventing influenza and influeza-like illness. Its effects on mortality for this age group as well as adverse events are uncertain.

An RCT of 31,989 adults 65 years and older compared a standard dose influenza vaccine (15 mcg hemagglutinin) with a high dose vaccine (60 mcg hemagglutinin) over two flu seasons. Laboratory confirmed influenza was less likely in the high dose group (1.4% vs. 1.9%, p < 0.05, NNT = 220). This small benefit must be balanced against a possibly higher risk of serious adverse events (3 vs. 0) and higher cost.

A trial randomized 9003 healthy adults 50 and older to a recombinant quadrivalent flu vaccine or inactivated quadrivalent flu vaccine. The recombinant vaccine provided a small advantage in terms of preventing flu (NNT = 100) in the study year.

A cluster randomized trial compared recombinant or standard dose flu vaccine in adults age 50 to 65 years. The number of cases of PCR-confirmed influenza was 2.0 cases/1000 persons in the high-dose group and 2.34 cases/1000 persons in the usual-dose group, or about 1 fewer case of influenza per 3000 persons. There was no difference in hospitalizations.

There remains uncertainty for the efficacy of high-dose influenza vaccine compared to standard dose vaccine. In one large industry-funded nonblinded RCT (GALFLU), high-dose vaccination provided a very small reduction in hospitalizations but had uncertain effect on hospitalization for pneumonia. The higher price of high-dose flu vaccine likely offsets the cost-effectiveness of this small benefit. A very similar Danish study (DANFLU) with 332,438 participants found no significant difference in hospitalization for the combined outcome of influenza or pneumonia.

A meta-analysis of 2 large population-based, industry-sponsored RCTs enrolling community-dwelling adults 65 years and older found high-dose influenca vaccine, as compared to standard dose vaccine, reduces hospitalizations for pneumonia or influenza (NNT=1,840) or cardiovascular events (NNT=731).

Influenza vaccination of healthy working adults under age 65 years can reduce the rates of febrile illness, lost workdays, and physician visits if there is a good match between the vaccine and the circulating virus. However, it does not reduce overall cost to society.

Live attenuated intranasal vaccine is approved for persons aged between 5 and 50 years. Some studies have shown that it may be safe and effective for younger children. However, it is not currently recommended due to evidence of poor effectiveness against H1N1 during the 2013-2014 and 2015-2016 influenza seasons.

An mRNA influenza vaccine was morslightly e effective than a standard vaccine at preventing influenza in adults 18 to 64 years old in a year whe(NNI = 300) n influenza A was dominant, but local and systemic adverse events were more prevalent with the mRNA vaccine.
Flu vaccine does not prevent asthma flares or acute otitis media in children.

Although baloxavir, zanamivir, laninamivir, and oseltamivir prevent symptomatic flu in close contacts and family members (NNT = 25-51), the cost and concerns about developing resistance argue against use for this indication, particularly in vaccinated individuals.

In the most recent study 2216 household contacts (all unvacccinated) were randomized to baloxavir or placebo. Baloxavir reduced the transmission of influenza virus to household contacts, but many of the persons with transmitted infections are asymptomatic. There was no significant reduction in symptomatic influenza among household contacts.

CDC guidelines recommend that persons with egg allergy who have had only hives after exposure to egg should receive the flu vaccine. Recombinant hemagglutinin influenza vaccine is egg-free and is recommended for adults 18 to 49 years. Many persons can safely receive influenza vaccination containing less than 1.2 mcg/ml egg protein, but appropriate precautions should still be taken and it should only be administered in a setting where patients can be observed for at least 30 minutes and emergency systems are in place in the event of a severe reaction. Live attenuated vaccine does contain egg protein. A cohort study in 779 persons age 2 to 18 years with egg allergy in the UK found no systemic reactions (95% CI, 0%-0.47% in all, 0%-1.4% in those with previous anaphylaxis). However, 8.1% experienced lower RTI symptoms, including 29 persons with wheeze.
Statins may impair the immune response to the vaccine, but the clinical implications of this are uncertain.
A vaccine to H7N9 (avian influenza) is under development.
A Cochrane review found no benefit of influenza vaccination in persons with cystic fibrosis, but the analysis was limited by a very small sample size (n = 179).

In children undergoing chemotherapy given the flu vaccine, they are able to generate an immune response (although weaker than in healthy children). Evidence of clinical effectiveness in this population is lacking.
Another Cochrane review of influenza vaccine for patients with hematologic malignancies found a reduction in the likelihood of lower respiratory tract infection and hospitalization with vaccination.
Very low- to low-certainty evidence suggests that influenza vaccination of immunosuppressed adults with cancer improves mortality and and infection-related outcomes.
For patients diagnosed with COPD, a Cochrane review found that influenza vaccine reduces the number of exacerbations (WMD −0.37; 95% CI, −0.64 to −0.11).
No trials were found in a Cochrane review of influenza vaccine for persons with bronchiectasis.

A meta-analysis found that flu vaccine was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events in adults with coronary disease, particularly those with a history of acute coronary syndrome within the past 6 months (NNT = 8).
An RCT with 2571 adults who had just been hospitalized with acute MI found that influenza vaccine reduced all cause mortality significantly in the next year (NNT = 50).

Among adults with periodontitis, chronic kidney disease, COPD, and CHF, influenza vaccination is associated with a decreased risk of developing dementia. And among adults with COPD or CHF, increased number of flu vaccinations confers progressive levels of protection against dementia.

An RCT in South Africa found that trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine significantly reduced the attack rates of influenza among HIV negative women (1.8% vs. 3.6%), the infants of HIV negative women (1.9% vs. 3.6%), and among HIV infected women (7.0% vs. 17.0%). Other Interventions Patient reminder and recall systems improve immunization rates (OR 2.2 for childhood influenza vaccination, 1.7 for adult influenza vaccination).Antibacterial household products do not reduce the risk of infectious symptoms.
There is no increase in flares when patients with rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, or spondylarthritis are given the flu vaccine.

Handwashing (especially around young children), isolation and social distancing may be effective at preventing the spread of influenza. A Cochrane review identified four studies of interventions to improve hand hygiene in healthcare settings, but only limited evidence of effectiveness. A systematic review found no evidence that N95 respirators are more effective than surgical masks at preventing influenza transmission. While N95 masks have theoretical advantages, they are also less comfortable which may impair usage. This was confirmed in a subsequent trial in 2862 healthcare personnel (8.2% vs 7.2%) laboratory confirmed flu.

A Cochrane review concluded that compared hand hygiene and masking with control for a range of respiratory viruses. The review has been criticized as the authors combined studies of masking for very different viruses. The overall risk of bias of studies was high, and adherence to the intervention was often low.
Patients with influenza classically present with rapid onset of fever, cough, chills or rigors, sore throat, and myalgias. B
Overall, physician judgment is useful with early but not late onset of symptoms. B

Rapid antigen tests are most useful during the shoulder season (beginning and end of the flu season), when the pretest probability of influenza is 5% to 10%. Their accuracy varies, with older tests having approximately 55% sensitivity compared to 80% to 95% for newer molecular tests.B

Differential.Differential_Features: Evidence of consolidation on physical examination and CXR
Hypoxia, tachycardia, and pleuritic chest pain common; fever uncommon

Differential.Differential_Name: Other viral lower respiratory tract infections
Differential.Differential_Features: Difficult to distinguish without laboratory investigation
Prominent myalgias and joint pains; conjunctivitis and rash with Zika

list.listitem: Patients classically present with rapid onset of fever, cough, chills or rigors, sore throat, and myalgias. Most studies of clinical diagnosis have included only patients with fever and cough, so their accuracy as predictors is underestimated in these studies.
The signs and symptoms most useful to help rule in influenza are fever, cough, rigors, onset of symptoms less than 3 days before office visit, and sweating.
Symptoms most helpful in ruling out influenza were no systemic symptoms, absence of coughing, being able to cope with daily activities, and not needing to be confined to bed.
Overall physician judgment was much better at diagnosing influenza when patients presented within 48 hours of symptom onset (LR+ 16.8 vs. 2.1, LR− 0.34 vs. 0.9) compared with later presentation.

A systematic review identified 162 studies (130 of rapid influenza diagnostic tests [RIDTs], 19 of digital immunoassays [DIAs], and 13 of rapid nucleic acid amplification tests [NAATs]). The older RIDTs had lower sensitivity (55%) than the newer DIAs (80%) and NAATs (92%); all tests had excellent specificity (98% or higher). This corresponds to very high positive likelihood ratios to rule-in influenza when any test is positive (LR+ 27-46), but varying negative likelihood ratios to rule-out flu when negative (0.46 for RIDT, 0.20 for DIA, and 0.08 for NAAT).

Rapid antigen tests are most useful during the shoulder season (beginning and end of the flu season) when the pretest probability of influenza is 5% to 10%. During flu season, patients with a negative rapid antigen test still have a significant likelihood of flu, so the test is less useful (see ).
Rapid antigen tests for H1N1 pandemic influenza has been shown to have reasonable sensitivity and specificity.
Confirmatory testing with PCR or culture is generally done only for disease surveillance.
A procalcitonin value <0.25 ng/ml (especially if <0.1) makes bacterial infection unlikely and during an influenza epidemic makes influenza correspondingly more likely.

Order CXR to rule out pneumonia in patients with lower respiratory tract findings or significant tachypnea or hypoxia. Two studies with approximately 2000 patients found no evidence that CXR improves clinical outcomes in patients with respiratory infection, though.
Consider pulmonary embolism in any patient with dyspnea, although fever makes it less likely.

Consider Dengue fever in areas where the disease is endemic (including southern Florida and the Keys), especially in patients with leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Also consider Chikungunya in Puerto Rico and Central and South America, and Zika Virus infection.

A "FluScore" decision rule has been developed and internally validated to classify patients at low, moderate, or high risk of influenza. It uses four patient reported symptoms: Fever + cough (2 points), Myalgias (2 points), Chills or sweats (1 point) or Sudden onset (1 point). The risk of influenza was 8% for 0 to 2 point, 30% for 3 points, and 59% for 4 or more points. Two-thirds of patients fell into the low or high risk groups, and required no further testing.

The FluScoreVax risk score for diagnosis of flu was developed using data from the large European GRACE trial and then validated in the US EAST-PC study. It has 6 items (subjective fever, interfered with usual activity, headache, wheeze, phlegm, and recent flu vaccine) and a range from -5 to 6 points. The AUC was 0.75 for both derivation and internal validation subgroups. The prevalence of flu in the low, moderate and high-risk groups was 6.8%, 21.8%, 35.3 in the external validation population.

A decision rule has been developed and validated to predict the need for hospitalization on mortality in patients presenting with acute respiratory infection. While not validated in a pandemic, it could be useful in such a setting.
See algorithm in .
Treatment is largely supportive with analgesics, antipyretics, rest, adequate (but not excessive) hydration, and reevaluation if symptoms worsen. C

Antiviral medications (oseltamivir, baloxavir, or zanamivir) are recommended only if the probability of influenza is high (see ) and patients present within 24 or at most 36 hours of symptoms onset. It is also recommended for pregnant patients and for hospitalized patients.A

Oseltamivir has not been shown in RCTs to reduce the likelihood of hospitalization or the likelihood of complications requiring antibiotics. Studies in patients with cardiopulmonary disease or in patients over age 65 years did not find a signficant reduction in the duration of symptoms. A

When given within 24 hours of the onset of symptoms, antiviral agents such as oseltamivir or zanamivir reduce the duration of symptoms by about 30 hours and may reduce the intensity somewhat. When given at 24 to 36 hours, it reduces duration by 14 hours. The overall reduction in the ITT population was 21 hours. A Cochrane review using ITT data also found a 21 hour reduction in symptoms.

There is no evidence from RCTs that oseltamivir reduces the likelihood of hospitalization or the likelihood of complications requiring antibiotics, once acute bronchitis is excluded as a complication. The likelihood of pneumonia was reduced by 0.9%, but only in patients with PCR or culture confirmed influenza, and not in the intention to treat population. Studies in patients with cardiopulmonary disease or in patients over age 65 years did not find a signficant reduction in the duration of symptoms. Much of these data were initially unpublished and analysis was based on unpublished clinical trial reports. The drugs are associated with an increased risk of nausea (NNH = 28) and vomiting (NNH = 22). A systematic review in 2025 showed similar findings, i.e. the use of antiviral medications (oseltamivir, baloxavir) in adults and children with nonsevere influenza does not reduce hospitalization or mortality and only has a modest effect on symptom duration.

An updated systematic review (2024) included several more studies than previous reviews and included unpublished studies. They found no evidence that oseltamivir reduces the likelihood of hospitalizations (1.3% vs 1.2%), even in high-risk or older patients, and has relatively common though nonserious harms. Another systematic review (2024) of 8 RCTs found low- to very low-certainty evidence that oseltamivir and peramivir may shorten hospital length of stay by 1.63 days and 1.73 days, respectively. Future analyses with more rigorous trials may have different findings.

2 RCTs comparing baloxavir with oseltamivir or placebo found a similar reduction in symptoms between oseltamivir and baloxavir compared to placebo (about 20-24 hours), with a greater benefit if given in the first 24 hours (33 hours fewer symptoms) than at 24 to 48 hours (13 hours). This is also similar to oseltamivir. Complications were not reported.
Usual dosing in adults is oseltamivir 75 mg po twice daily for 5 days, baloxavir 40 mg (< 80 kg) or 80 mg (> 80 kg) in a single dose, or zanamivir 10 mg by MDI bid for 5 days.

A study randomized 366 hospitalized patients with severe influenza to baloxavir plus oseltamivir, zanamivir or peramivir, or to oseltamivir, zanamivir, or peramivir alone. There was no difference in time to symptom improvement (97.5 vs 100 hours) or any other outcomes.

A Cochrane review found that amantadine and rimantadine were both effective for the prevention and treatment of influenza symptoms. However, the drugs have significant adverse effects (especially amantadine) and widespread resistance exists. They should not be used routinely in practice, based on current CDC recommendations.

A Cochrane review identified one RCT and 29 observational studies of corticosteroids for influenza. The RCT was too small to provide useful information. In the observational studies, there was an association with increased mortality but this could represent residual confounding and confounding by indication, as sicker patients and patients with ARDS or other complications were preferentially given corticosteroids.
In hospitalized patients with flu and a pulmonary infiltrate, an RCT found that adding clarithromycin and naproxen reduced 30 day mortality (0.9% vs. 8.2%; p = 0.01; NNT = 14) and 90-day mortality.

A randomized trial randomized 633 patients with influenza who were at increased risk of complications to either the combination of oseltamivir, amantadine, and ribavrin or to oseltamivir alone. There was some reduction in viral shedding with the combination therapy, but no reduction in influenza symptom severity or duration. There was no difference in adverse events.
Two poor-quality RCTs provide insufficient evidence to recommend "Ganmao" or "E Shu You" Chinese herbal medicines for influenza.
Two poor-quality RCTs found a small benefit to the homeopathic drug oscillococcinum; current evidence is insufficient to recommend this intervention routinely.
Treatment generally includes rest, fluids, and antipyretics. "Forcing fluids" is not supported by any clinical studies and may lead to hyponatremia, especially in infants and the elderly.
Supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation may be needed for hospitalized patients.

In a cohort study of 343 Welsh patients with influenza, complications included bronchitis (19%; 95% CI, 15%-23%), pneumonia (2.9%; 95% CI, 1.4%-5.4%), otitis media (2.3%; 95% CI, 1.0%-4.6%). See those chapters for management of those conditions.

Influenza may also worsen cardiac disease and diabetes mellitus control in affected individuals.In a U.S. cohort study, up to 12% of adults hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed influenza from 2000 to 2018 experienced acute heart failure or acute coronary syndrome.

In a case-control study of 119 hospitalized patients and 196 matched controls, risk factors for hospitalization included COPD, more than one significant comorbidty, polypharmacy, more than 5 GP consultations in the previous year, and previous hospitalizations in patients aged 18 to 64 years. B
In the same study, risk factors for patients over age 65 years were all of the above plus CHF and minus previous hospitalizations. B

A clinical decision rule was developed in 16,280 patients and validated in over 11,000 patients to predict the likelihood of hospitalization or pneumonia or death from any cause during flu season in community-dwelling elderly (aged 65 years and older). Key factors include age, previous hospitalization, comorbidities, gender, and number of outpatient visits in the previous year (). A

The 30-day mortality rate for patients with influenza presenting to the emergency department of 6 Swedish hospitals was 2.5%, compared to 6% for those presenting with RSV and 7.9% for those presenting with COVID-19 (Omicron variant). Influenza and RSV mortality rates were similar before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. B
Oseltamivir provided very little benefit as prophylaxis for older patients who had received influenza vaccine.

Investigators analyzed data obtained from birth registries in Canada for all live births occurring between October 2010 and March 2014 with follow-up to March 2016. Multiple adjustments occurred to control for maternal medical history and other potential confounders. From a total of 28,255 children, 10,227 were born to women who received a seasonal influenza vaccination during pregnancy. This study found no evidence of an increased risk of adverse childhood health outcomes with maternal influenza vaccination during pregnancy.

Similarly, a large cohort study in South Korea during the COVID-19 pandemic found no association between influenza vaccination during pregnancy and preeclampsia, antenatal bleeding, premature/low birth weight, congenital defects, or neonatal mortality.

Likelihood of hospitalization for flu was 7 per 10,000 child-years in an urban cohort. A history of cardiac and neuromuscular conditions was an independent predictor for hospitalization. Median age of hospitalization was 1.8 years.
Oseltamivir is approved for children over age 1 year. Dosing is 75 mg bid if >40 kg or 13 years old, 60 mg bid if 23 to 40 kg, 45 mg bid if 15 to 23 kg, and 30 mg bid if ≤5 kg.
Zanamivir is approved for children aged 7 years and older is 10 mg by metered-dose inhaler twice daily.
Rimantadine is not FDA approved for treatment of influenza in children.

cell.label: Patient with suspected influenza (fever, cough and/or myalgias); presentation within 48 hours of illness onset?
Further evaluation guided by relationship to flu season.
∼2% pretest probability of influenza: consider rapid flu test only if flu, otherwise likely due to severity of symptoms or recent exposure.
5%-10% pretest probability of flu: order rapid flu test.
1%-3% probability of flu: supportive treatment with adequate hydration, analgesics, and followup.
49%-67% probability of flu; initiate antiviral medication.
30%-50% pretest probability of flu: consider empiric therapy with antiviral medication vs. rapid flu test; result if flu test chosen?
11%-22% probability of flu: supportive treatment with adequate hydration, analgesics, and followup.
89%-95% probability of flu: initiate antiviral medication.
Supportive treatment with analgesics, adequate hydration, and follow-up; CXR to rule out pneumonia if lower respiratory tract symptoms.
